# Warren Buffett: "The Superinvestors of Graham-and-Doddsville" (1984)

Source: [The Superinvestors of Graham-and-Doddsville](../../../../../Publications/The%20Superinvestors%20of%20Graham-and-Doddsville%20_%20Columbia%20Business%20School.md)

Note: Buffett wrote this for the 50th anniversary of *Security Analysis* (Columbia Business School, published May 17, 1984). It answers the efficient-market claim that investors who beat the market are just lucky. Use it for **evaluating whether a manager's record reflects skill, the price-vs-value discipline, and why lower price means lower risk**. It complements [buffett.md](../Invesotrs/buffett.md) and [graham.md](../Invesotrs/graham.md).

## 1. The Coin-Flipping Argument [verified]

- Suppose 225 million Americans each bet $1 on a daily coin flip, and the losers drop out.
  - After 10 days, about 220,000 people have called 10 flips in a row, winning a little over $1,000 each.
  - After 20 days, 215 remain, each having turned $1 into a little over $1 million.
- The same result would come from 225 million orangutans. Pure chance produces a few spectacular records.
- **What matters is concentration.** If 40 of the 215 winning orangutans came from one zoo in Omaha, "you would be pretty sure you were on to something". Likewise, 400 cases of a rare cancer in one small Montana mining town point to a cause.
- Buffett's claim is that a disproportionate number of winners came from one "intellectual village": Graham-and-Doddsville.
- **Ruling out copying.** Concentration means nothing if 100 followers simply copy one leader's calls. The Graham-and-Dodd investors share a theory, but "each student has decided on his own manner of applying the theory." Their portfolios had very low overlap.

## 2. Conditions That Make a Record Meaningful [verified]

- The managers were "pre-identified as superior investors, the most recent identification occurring over fifteen years ago." If he had just searched thousands of records for winners, "I would advise you to stop reading right here."
- The records were audited, and the checks received by investors matched the stated records.
- He chose them "based upon their framework for investment decision-making", knowing "what they had been taught" plus their "intellect, character, and temperament."
- For the pension funds, these were "the only two I have influenced", not picked from dozens.

## 3. The Common Theme [verified]

- They "search for discrepancies between the *value* of a business and the *price* of small pieces of that business in the market."
- They ignore the day of the week or the month. They "do not discuss beta, the capital asset pricing model, or covariance in returns." They "simply focus on two variables: price and value."
- Price-and-volume studies get done because the data exist, not because they are useful: "to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail."
- "Mentally, *always buying the business, not buying the stock*." Some hold dozens of stocks and others a handful, "but all exploit the difference between the market price of a business and its intrinsic value."

## 4. The Records [verified]

| Manager / vehicle | Period | Result | Benchmark | Style note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Walter Schloss (WJS Partnership) | 28¼ yrs to 1984 Q1 | 21.3%/yr partnership (16.1% limited partners) | S&P 8.4%/yr | Over 800 issues owned; usually 100+ positions; "looks up the numbers in the manuals" |
| Tweedy, Browne (TBK) | 15¾ yrs, 1968–1983 | 20.0%/yr overall (16.0% LPs) | S&P 7.0%/yr | Very wide diversification; passive holdings did as well as control positions |
| Buffett Partnership | 1957–1969 | 29.5%/yr partnership (23.8% LPs) | Dow 7.4%/yr | "The best thing he did was to quit in 1969" |
| Sequoia Fund (Bill Ruane) | July 1970–1984 Q1 | 17.2%/yr (18.2% gross of 1% fee) | S&P 10.0%/yr | Started in the two-tier market; Buffett's only recommendation to his partners |
| Charlie Munger partnership | 1962–1975 | 19.8%/yr overall (13.7% LPs) | Dow 5.0%/yr | Concentrated, more volatile; −31.9% in 1973 and −31.5% in 1974 |
| Rick Guerin (Pacific Partners) | 1965–1983 | 32.9%/yr overall (23.6% LPs) | S&P 7.8%/yr | Ex-IBM salesman, math major |
| Stan Perlmeter | 8/1965–10/1983 | 23.0%/yr overall (19.0% LPs) | Dow about 7%/yr | Former ad-agency partner |
| Washington Post pension (3 value managers) | to 1983 | Master Trust top percentile across periods | A.C. Becker universe | Required to hold at least 25% bonds |
| FMC pension | from 1974 | No. 1 in the Becker survey for its size | Large-plan median | $243M above the median result |

- Schloss: "if a business is worth a dollar and I can buy it for 40 cents, something good may happen to me." His strength is that "no one has much influence on him."
- Munger's holdings were "almost completely different" from the others'. FMC's managers were not Buffett's picks but shared "the common denominators of selecting securities based on value."
- **Down markets:** "this group has assumed far less risk than average; note their record in years when the general market was weak." For example, in the S&P's 1974 fall of −26.6%, Schloss lost −6.2%. Tweedy, Browne made +1.5% while the S&P fell −38.1% in its September 1974 year.

## 5. Size and Performance [verified]

- "Size is the anchor of performance. There is no question about it. It doesn't mean you can't do better than average when you get larger, but the margin shrinks."
- Managing an amount equal to the total market value means you cannot beat the average.
- Ruane's expectation set in advance: a 4-point annual edge over the S&P "would be solid performance."

## 6. Risk vs. Reward in Value Investing [verified]

- With a six-shooter offer, more risk earns more reward: a positive correlation.
- "The exact opposite is true with value investing. If you buy a dollar bill for 60 cents, it's riskier than if you buy a dollar bill for 40 cents, but the expectation of reward is greater in the latter case. The greater the potential for reward in the value portfolio, the less risk there is."
- **Washington Post, 1973:**
  - Market value was $80M, while the assets could have been sold to any of ten buyers for at least $400M. Those properties were worth $2B by 1984.
  - Had the price fallen to $40M, its beta would have risen, making it look "riskier." "This is truly Alice in Wonderland."
  - Buying ten such $40M piles for $8M each carries "essentially no risk," provided the managers are honest and reasonably competent.
- **Margin of safety:** "You don't try and buy businesses worth $83 million for $80 million. You leave yourself an enormous margin. When you build a bridge, you insist it can carry 30,000 pounds, but you only drive 10,000 pound trucks across it."

## 7. Market Efficiency and Persistence [verified]

- When prices are set "at the margin by the most emotional person, or the greediest person, or the most depressed person, it is hard to argue that the market always prices rationally. In fact, market prices are frequently nonsensical."
- The value idea "takes immediately to people or it doesn't take at all. It's like an inoculation... I've never seen anyone who became a gradual convert over a ten-year period."
- The secret has been out for 50 years, yet he has seen "no trend toward value investing in the 35 years that I've practiced it." "Ships will sail around the world but the Flat Earth Society will flourish."

## 8. Manager / Track-Record Evaluation Checklist

1. **Selected in advance?** Was the manager identified before the record was made, or picked after the fact from thousands (survivorship)?
2. **Audited and real?** Are the results audited and matched by actual investor cash flows?
3. **Coherent framework?** Can the manager explain buying based on price vs. business value, not momentum, calendar effects, or beta?
4. **Independent?** Do holdings differ from peers' and from benchmarks, or is it a crowd following one signal?
5. **Down-market behavior.** Compare results in weak years. Value records should show smaller losses. Concentrated styles (Munger, Guerin) can still have deep drawdowns.
6. **Fees.** Compare limited-partner or net returns, not gross. Note the gaps in the table above.
7. **Size.** Has assets under management grown to the point where the edge must shrink?
8. **Margin of safety in each holding.** Look for a large gap, not marginal undervaluation (the $83M vs. $80M example).
9. **Management integrity.** When buying assets at a discount, check that the stewards are "honest and reasonably competent people."

## 9. Key Quotes

- "The investors simply focus on two variables: price and value."
- "Always buying the business, not buying the stock."
- "The greater the potential for reward in the value portfolio, the less risk there is."
- "Size is the anchor of performance."
- "You leave yourself an enormous margin."
